text: Βαπτισθῆναι ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ Ἰορδάνῃ. Quo de more Eusebius, De vita Constantini, lib. iv, cap. 62. Eusebius et Hieronymus, De locis Hebraicis, auctor Vitæ sancti Basilii, apud Amphilochium, cap. 4; Theodoritus, Hist. eccl. lib. i, cap. 32; Joannes Moschus noster, cap. 176; Alexander Monachus, in Gretsero, De cruce, c. 1231 D. Quibus adde Itinerarium Antonini, cum Hodæporico, sancti Willibaldi.
anchorLine: σιν αὐτὸν βαπτισθῆναι ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ Ἰορδάνῃ (z).
en: On being baptized in the holy Jordan. On this custom see Eusebius, Life of Constantine, bk. 4, ch. 62; Eusebius and Jerome, On Hebrew Places; the author of the Life of St Basil, in Amphilochius, ch. 4; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, bk. 1, ch. 32; our John Moschus, ch. 176; Alexander the Monk, in Gretser, On the Cross, col. 1231 D. To these add the Itinerary of Antoninus, with the Hodoeporicon of St Willibald.

text: Ἔνιψεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας. Quod spectat ad loturam pedum, afferam insignem ad Origenem emendationem, tom. 32, in Joannem p. 347-375: Καὶ ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς γε ἐν τούτοις μοι δοκεῖ διεγείρων ἡμῶν τὸν νοῦν ἐπὶ τῶν νοερῶν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον, μὴ τετηρηκέναι μὲν σωματικὴν περὶ τοῦ νίψασθαι τὴν ἀκολουθίαν. Ita edidit præstantissimus et celeberrimus vir Petrus Daniel Huetius, conjectura facta ex hisce codicis Reg. Ἐν τοὺς μοι δοκεῖ. Mihi vero perplacet, ἔνθους μοι. Et verto: Quin et evangelista numine afflatus, videtur mihi, excitans mentem nostram ad intelligentiam spiritualem præsentis loci, non observasse corporalem lavandi consequentiam. Vita Joannis Chrysostomi, ab incerto seu anonymo scripta, p. 324, l. xxi, loco insigni, obscuro, per doctissimum clarissimumque Savilium non intellecto, et eapropter apponendo hic: Τούτοις ὁ μέγας καταπλαγεὶς, καὶ ἔνθους ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰρημένοις γενόμενος, ἀνεσκόπει· καὶ γάρ πως ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ χρηματιζόμενον. Id est, His magnus ille perculsus, et velut ad ea verba divinitus inspiratus, considerabat. Ipsius etenim anima quodammodo admonebatur. Sed ut ad rem redeam, quid sit balatoforum in testamento sancti Remigii, apud Flodoardum, lib. i, cap. 28, nemo, quod sciam, docuit: Aliis pauperibus tribus, ubi fratres quotidie pedes lavare debent, quibus etiam balatoforum, quod dicitur, xenodochium, ad hoc ministerium statui, solidus unus dabitur. Nec ego possum explicare monstrum lectionis; duntaxat possum per conjecturam corrigere, scribendo balnaforum aut balaneophorum, βαλανειοφόρον, quod ita a balneo et lavacro dictum sit.
anchorLine: ἐνέγκας ὕδωρ, ἔνιψεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας (a), καὶ δι'
en: On 'He washed his feet.' As regards the washing of feet, I shall bring forward a notable emendation of Origen, vol. 32, On John, pp. 347-375: [Greek: the evangelist, it seems to me, in these things, rousing our mind to the spiritual realities of the place, did not observe the bodily sequence concerning the washing]. So the most distinguished and celebrated Pierre-Daniel Huet edited it, by a conjecture made from these words of the Royal codex, 'Ἐν τοὺς μοι δοκεῖ.' To me 'ἔνθους μοι' is preferable. And I translate: 'Indeed the evangelist too, inspired by the divine breath, seems to me to be rousing our mind to the spiritual understanding of the present passage, and not to have observed the bodily order of the washing.' In the Life of John Chrysostom, written by an unknown or anonymous author, p. 324, l. 21, a notable passage which the most learned and illustrious Savile did not understand and which is therefore added here: [Greek: Struck by these things, and as though inspired by what had been said, he reflected; for his soul in some way ...the oracle]. That is: 'Greatly struck by these things, and as if divinely inspired by those words, he pondered. For his soul was in a way being admonished.' But to return to the matter, nobody to my knowledge has explained what 'balatoforum' is in the testament of St Remigius, in Flodoard, bk. 1, ch. 28: 'To three other poor persons, where the brothers daily must wash feet, to whom also of the balatoforum, as it is called, of the xenodochium, I have appointed for this service one solidus.' I cannot explain the monstrous reading, but I can only correct it by conjecture, writing 'balnaforum' or 'balaneophorum' (βαλανειοφόρον), so called from bath and washing-place.

text: Βλάπτειν. Non sine indignatione leges ista apud Cyrillum ad Joan. xii, 46, p. 691: Καὶ ἵνα αὐτοὶ μὴ ἰσχύοντες βλέψαι τὸν οὐδὲν ἀδικήσαντα, τοὺς δυνατωτέρους κατ' αὐτοῦ ἐρεθίσωσι· Utque cum ipsi non possent in os intueri eum qui nihil injustum fecerat, potentiores adversus eum irritarent atque accenderent. Quanta enim ἀβλεψία, non percepisse βλάψαι, lædere eum qui nulla injuria affecerat.
anchorLine: ἢ τίς ἰσχύει βλάπτειν (b);
en: 'To harm.' You will not read this without indignation in Cyril on John 12:46, p. 691: [Greek: And so that they themselves, being unable to look upon the man who had done no wrong, might stir up the more powerful against him]; that is, since they could not look in the face the one who had done nothing unjust, they would provoke and inflame the more powerful against him. How great the blindness, not to have grasped what it is to harm one who has done no injury.

text: Τῶν ἔμπροσθεν. Philipp. iii, 14: Ἓν δέ, τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθανόμενος, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος, κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Unum autem, quæ quidem retro sunt obliviscens, ad ea vero quæ sunt priora extendens meipsum, ad destinatum persequor, ad bravium supernæ vocationis Dei in Christo Jesu. Ad quæ respiciens Cæsarius, quæst. 171, scripserat: Ὁ γὰρ πολὺς ἐκεῖνος καὶ ὑψηλὸς τὴν διάνοιαν, ἀεὶ διὰ ταύτης θέων οὐδέποτε τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος ἔληξεν. Hoc est, Magnus enim ille et mente excelsus, per hanc (virtutem) perpetuo currens, nunquam ad ea quæ priora sunt extendere se cessavit. At bellis hominibus placuit edere ἐπεκτεινομένοις ἔλεξεν, cum hac versione sua, nunquam ad ulteriora se pervenisse dixit. I nunc, et linguæ Græcæ notitiam neglige, ut editionibus fideas, auctores Græcos intelligas.
anchorLine: βλέποντες εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, τῶν ἔμπροσθεν (b') ἐπιλαν-
en: 'Of the things before.' Philippians 3:14: [quoted in Greek and Latin: one thing, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus]. Caesarius, question 171, had written with this in view: [Greek: for that great man, lofty in mind, running always through this virtue, never ceased stretching forward to what lies ahead]. That is: that great man, exalted in mind, running continually by this (virtue), never ceased to stretch himself toward the things that were before. But certain fine people saw fit to print 'ἐπεκτεινομένοις ἔλεξεν', and with this translation of theirs said that he never reached anything further. Go on then, and neglect knowledge of Greek, so that you may trust the editions and understand the Greek authors!

text: Τὸν ἀρχιδιακόνου εἴσοδον. Vel τοῦ, vel τήν.
anchorLine: ἐμήνυσας τὴν ἀρχιδιακόνου εἴσοδον (c), ἀλλ' οὕτως
en: 'The entrance of the archdeacon' (accusative 'τὸν'): alternatively 'τοῦ' or 'τήν'.

text: Ἀμηνυτί. Adverbium lexicis addendum, quod etiam reperi in N.li Opusculis, p. 379, clarumque est ex similibus multis, ut est ἀνιδρωτί. Hoc sæpe occurrit, et reddi debet Cyrillo in Isaiam, p. 808 B, ubi contraria, ut sententia, sic dictione, σὺν ἱδρῶτι.
anchorLine: τὴν τάξιν, ἀρχιδιάκονε Ἰουλιανέ, ἀλλ' ἀμηνυτί (d)
en: 'Ἀμηνυτί' (without announcing). An adverb to be added to the lexicons, which I also found in the Opuscula of N[ilus], p. 379, and whose meaning is clear from many similar forms, such as 'ἀνιδρωτί'. It occurs often, and ought to be restored in Cyril on Isaiah, p. 808 B, where the opposite, in sense as in wording, is 'σὺν ἱδρῶτι' (with sweat).

text:
Βαΐν, seu βαΐον. Remittam te ad alios, ubi posuero scholium seu observatiunculam cod. Reg. 1067, f. 212.
Βαΐα διὰ τί λέγονται οἱ κλάδοι τῶν φοινίκων; Ἐπειδὴ τῇ Ἑβραίων φωνῇ ἡ σελήνη βαΐον ὀνομάζεται. Ὁ γοῦν φοῖνιξ τὸ δένδρον καθ' ἑκάστην πρόοδον τῆς σελήνης, ἣν τινες γένναν καλοῦσιν, ἐκ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ καρδίας ἀναδίδωσι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τούτους τοὺς κλάδους τῶν φοινίκων, Ἑβραῖοι, βαΐα προσαγορεύουσιν· ἀπὸ τοῦ περὶ τὸ δένδρον συμβαίνοντος παραδόξου κατωνομάζοντες. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐξ ἐκείνων παραλαβόντες, καλοῦμεν αὐτὰ βαΐα.
Quamobrem rami palmarum, βαΐα dicuntur? Quia Hebræorum lingua luna nominatur βαΐον. Itaque palma arbor, quolibet lunæ processu, quem nonnulli nativitatem vocant, ex suo corde ramos producit: eaque de causa ramos illos palmarum, Hebræi βαΐα nuncupant; ab inopino quod arbori contingit denominantes. Simili ratione et nos ab illis accipientes βαΐα indigitamus.
Aliter Callistus in Synaxario: Ἐδήλουν δὲ διὰ τῶν βαΐων, οἱονεὶ τῶν κλάδων. Βαΐον γὰρ παρ' Ἑβραίοις ὁ ἁπλοῦς κλάδος λέγεται. In Triodio Græcorum, τῶν βαΐων Sabbato, βαΐον παρ' Ἑβραίοις ὁ ἁπαλὸς κλάδος λέγεται. Grammatici Græci deducunt, παρὰ τὸ βίᾳ τίλλεσθαι. Balsamoni vox latina est, aliis Ægyptia. Sed quis nescit nugas etymologistarum? Chronici Alexandrini vocati, p. 7821: Καὶ προσῆλθεν τῷ βασιλεῖ Οὐαλεντινιανῷ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ βαΐῳ πρωΐ. Lege vel σὺν τῷ βαΐῳ, vel βαΐων. Et accessit mulier cum palma mane ad imperatorem Valentinianum. Aut: Et accessit ad imperatorem Valentinianum mulier mane festi Palmarum.
anchorLine: τοῦ τὸ βαΐν (f), ἀνέστησαν οἱ τοῦ μέρους αὐτοῦ κρά-
en: 'Baïn' or 'baïon.' I shall refer you to others, where I have set down a scholium or little observation from Royal codex 1067, f. 212. [Scholium:] Why are the branches of palm trees called baia? Because in the Hebrew tongue the moon is called baion. The palm tree, at each advance of the moon (which some call the 'birth'), puts forth branches from its own heart; and for that reason the Hebrews call these palm branches baia, naming them from the marvel that happens to the tree. Likewise we, having received them from those people, call them baia. [Latin version of the same.] Otherwise, Callistus in the Synaxarion: 'They signified by the baia, as it were, the branches. For among the Hebrews the simple branch is called baion.' In the Triodion of the Greeks, on the Sabbath of the palms: 'baion among the Hebrews is the tender branch.' The Greek grammarians derive it from 'to be plucked by force.' Balsamon says it is a Latin word, others say Egyptian. But who does not know the follies of the etymologists? The so-called Alexandrian Chronicle, p. 7821: 'And the wife came to the emperor Valentinian with the palm early in the morning.' Read either 'with the palm' or 'of the palms.' And a woman came with a palm in the morning to the emperor Valentinian; or: and a woman came to the emperor Valentinian on the morning of Palm Sunday.

text: Βουκίνου, βούκινον et βύκινον, buccina. Unde βουκινάτωρ et βυκινάτωρ. Juris Græco Romani, p. 49, βικινάτωρ, sed præstat βυκινάτωρ, ut p. 232, et 506; necnon apud Blastarem, p. 72 E.
anchorLine: ἀκούει φωνῆς βουκίνου (g) ὡς ἐν πολέμῳ
en: 'Boukinou', 'boukinon' and 'bykinon': a trumpet (buccina). Hence 'boukinator' and 'bykinator' (trumpeter). In the Jus Graeco-Romanum, p. 49, 'bikinator', but 'bykinator' is preferable, as on pp. 232 and 506; also in Blastares, p. 72 E.

text: Καταρώμεθα. In Zachariam Cyrillus, p. 673 D. Τοῦτό τι παθεῖν ἐπειρᾶτό τινα τῶν εἰς Χριστὸν δεδυσσεβηκότων ὁ μακάριος Δαβίδ, λέγων· Καὶ διάβολος στήτω ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτοῦ. Sed non dubito quin scripserit ἐπηρᾶτο. Ad hunc sensum: Hoc ut contingeret cuidam in Christum impiorum, imprecabatur beatus David dicens: « Diabolus stet a dextris ejus. » Psal. cviii, 6, de Juda. Parque mendum offendes in Anastasii quæst. 62, p. 410: Τί δὲ οἱ θαυμάσιοι Πέτρος καὶ Παῦλος; οὐχὶ ὁ μὲν θάνατον ἐπὶ Ἀνανίαν καὶ Σαπφείραν ἐπήγαγεν; ὁ δὲ πήρωσιν Ἐλύμᾳ τῷ μάγῳ ἐπαγόμενος (imo ἐπαρώμενος vel cum cod. Reg. 1789, ἐπαρασάμενος) ἐπήνεγκε: Quid vero admirabiles illi Petrus et Paulus? Annon ille mortem attulit Ananiæ et Saphiræ? Hic autem, Elymam magum exsecratus orbavit oculis?
anchorLine: μεθα (h). Ὡς ὅταν λέγομεν· « Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός,
en: 'We curse.' Cyril on Zechariah, p. 673 D: [Greek: the blessed David tried to bring this upon one of those who had been impious toward Christ, saying: 'Let the devil stand at his right hand']. But I do not doubt that he wrote 'ἐπηρᾶτο.' To this sense: that this might befall one of the impious against Christ, blessed David was calling down a curse, saying 'Let the devil stand at his right hand' (Ps. 108:6), about Judas. You will find the same fault in Anastasius, question 62, p. 410: [Greek: And what of the wondrous Peter and Paul? Did not the one bring death on Ananias and Sapphira, and the other, inflicting blindness on Elymas the magician (rather 'invoking a curse', or with Royal codex 1789 'having cursed'), bring it about?] That is: What of those admirable men Peter and Paul? Did not Peter bring death on Ananias and Sapphira? And did not Paul, cursing Elymas the magician, deprive him of sight?

text: Ἐπίτασις. Corrupte apud Cyrillum, ad Joan. xiii, 6, t. IV, p. 722 D, impressum est στάσιν pro τάσιν. Τὸ ἀπονίζεσθαι τοὺς πόδας, μετρίως ἀποχαλᾷ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ βαδίσματος τάσιν· Pedum ablutio aliquantum relaxat et resolvit distensionem ex incessu ortam. Item in Epistolis Nili, lib. III, epist. 142, ἀνάστασιν pro ἀνάτασιν· Καὶ πάντως ἐπάνω φανείημεν τῆς δυσθυμίας, τῆς δολουργῶς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκαθάρτων πνευμάτων ἡμῖν ὑποσπειρομένης, πρὸς τὸ παραλῦσαι ἡμῶν καὶ ἐκνευρίσαι τὴν δικαίαν ἀνάτασιν· Et omnino supra tristitiam esse appareamus, quæ in nobis insidiose ab impuris spiritibus disseminatur, ad dissolvendam et enervandam justam nostram contentionem. Editio Possini epist. 99, Ἔννοιαν.
anchorLine: ἀδελφοί· ἀλλ' ἡ τῆς ἀσκήσεως ἐπίτασις (j) ἀποσβεν-
en: 'Intensity.' Corruptly in Cyril, on John 13:6, vol. 4, p. 722 D, 'στάσιν' is printed for 'τάσιν'. [Greek: Washing the feet moderately relaxes the strain from walking.] That is: the washing of the feet relaxes somewhat and loosens the strain arising from walking. Likewise in the Letters of Nilus, bk. 3, letter 142, 'ἀνάστασιν' for 'ἀνάτασιν': [Greek quoted]: and let us by all means appear above the despondency craftily sown in us by unclean spirits to loosen and unnerve our rightful striving. The edition of Possinus, letter 99, has 'Ἔννοιαν'.

text: Hoc epithetum vir omni laude major Carolus Fresnius, in Dissertatione de inferioris ævi numismatibus, cap. 67, ponit in nummo Heraclii: longe rectius quam ii qui legendum putaverant, λογοθέτης, νομοθέτης. Quanquam ἀθλοθέτης propius accedit ad ectypum; ut cuilibet patebit.
anchorLine: δόξα, καὶ ταύτην ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης (k) τοῖς ἀγωνιζομέ-
en: This epithet Charles Du Fresne (Du Cange), a man above all praise, in his Dissertation on the coinage of the later age, ch. 67, places on a coin of Heraclius: far more correctly than those who thought one should read 'logothetes' or 'nomothetes'. Although 'athlothetes' comes closer to the impression, as will be plain to anyone.

text: Ἠνέσχετο. Hom. 25, Paschali sancti Cyrilli, p. 299 C: Οἱ γὰρ ἀκάθεκτοι πρὸς πλεονεξίαν, ἀεὶ τοῖς οὖσι προστιθέναι σπουδάζοντες τὰ οὐκ αὐτοῖς μᾶλλον, τοῖς δὲ πέλας προσήκοντα, τάχα που καὶ μόνοι τὴν γῆν οἰκήσιμον ἔχειν ἐπείγονται, γειτόνων οὐκ ἀνεχόμενοι. Non ἀπεχόμενοι: Qui enim immoderata cupiditate habendi laborant, semper iis quæ possident adjicere studentes ea quæ ad vicinos potius, quam ad ipsos spectant, quodammodo soli habitare terram conantur, qui finitimos pati non possint.
anchorLine: ἠνέσχετό (l) ποτε, ἵνα ἄλλος αὐτῷ γεμίσει ὕδωρ·
en: 'He endured.' Paschal Homily 25 of St Cyril, p. 299 C: [Greek: for those unrestrained in greed, always eager to add to what they have what is not theirs, and rather what belongs to their neighbours, perhaps even strive to hold the habitable land alone, not tolerating neighbours]. [The editor notes 'Not ἀπεχόμενοι' (not 'refraining').] Latin: For those who labour under immoderate desire of having, always eager to add to what they possess what pertains to their neighbours rather than to themselves, in a way try to inhabit the earth alone, since they cannot bear neighbours.

text: Ἐσχόλαζεν εἰς τὰ καλιγραφία. Infra Balsamon, De jejuniis, n. 21: Ποῖος κανὼν ταύτας ἐκαλιγράφησε; Καλλιγραφίας δυσδιόρθωτον τέχνην appellat auctor Vitæ Nili junioris, p. 57. Et in Anastasii Hodego, p. 204, ubi habetur: Πρὸς Γεώργιον τὸν πρεσβύτερον, καὶ λογογράφον τῆς ἐκκλησίας αὐτῶν, τὸν λεγόμενον Κλειδοποιόν. Exemplar Regium 1052 καλλιγράφον exhibet atque καχθιδοποιόν; Juris Græco-Romani p. 1, p. 470, καλλιγραφήσαντας ἢ καχιγραφήσαντας; actione 14 sextæ synodi, καλῶς καλλιγραφεῖ.
anchorLine: ὀλίγα βιβλία· ἐσχόλαζεν δὲ εἰς τὰ καλιγραφία (m).
en: 'He was occupied with calligraphy.' See below, Balsamon, On Fasts, n. 21: 'What canon wrote these out in a fair hand?'; the author of the Life of Nilus the Younger, p. 57, calls it 'the art of calligraphy, hard to correct'. And in Anastasius's Hodegos, p. 204, where we find: 'To George the presbyter and scribe of their church, called the Locksmith (Kleidopoios).' The Royal copy 1052 offers 'kalligraphon' and 'kathidopoion'; Jus Graeco-Romanum, part 1, p. 470, 'those who had written fair' or 'kachigraphesantas'; in action 14 of the sixth synod, 'he writes well'.
